en jakke.explanation: "En jakke" is a jacket. In Denmark the weather often changes, so people carry one a lot: "Tag en jakke med" means "bring a jacket". A thicker, longer one is "en frakke", which means a coat.

sentence.da: Tag din **jakke** på, det er koldt.
sentence.en: Put your jacket on, it is cold.

en julegave.explanation: "En julegave" is a Christmas present, from "jul" and "gave" (gift). In Denmark gifts are opened on Christmas Eve, the evening of the 24th, not on Christmas morning. Danes often say "at købe julegaver" for Christmas shopping.

sentence.da: Jeg har købt en **julegave** til min mor.
sentence.en: I have bought a Christmas present for my mother.

et job.explanation: "Et job" is a job, and it is borrowed from English. Note that "jobbet" has two b's when "the" is added. The plural is the same as the singular. "Et arbejde" means about the same, and "at have et job" means to have a job.

sentence.en: I have a new job.

et jordbær.explanation: "Et jordbær" is a strawberry. It is built from "jord" (earth, ground) and "bær" (berry). Notice that the plural is the same as the single form: "et jordbær" becomes "mange jordbær". Strawberries are a big part of Danish summer.

sentence.da: Om sommeren spiser vi **jordbær** med fløde.
sentence.en: In the summer we eat strawberries with cream.

et juletræ.explanation: "Et juletræ" is a Christmas tree, from "jul" and "træ" (tree). In Denmark the tree is usually put up shortly before Christmas Eve and decorated with hearts, flags and often real candles. Families sing and dance around it on the evening of the 24th.

sentence.en: We are decorating the Christmas tree today.

ja.explanation: "Ja" means "yes" and is used just like in English. "Ja tak" is "yes please" and is the polite way to accept an offer. You will often hear "jaja" or "ja ja" in a relaxed way. If someone asks a negative question, Danes answer "jo" instead, not "ja".

sentence.da: **Ja**, jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe.
sentence.en: Yes, I would like a cup of coffee.

januar.explanation: "Januar" is January, the first month. It is an et-word, but you almost always use it without "et" and say "i januar" (in January). Month names are written with a small letter in Danish. Use "i begyndelsen af januar" for early January and "midt i januar" for mid-January.

sentence.en: It is cold in January.

japan.explanation: "Japan" is Japan. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Japan" means "in Japan" and "til Japan" means "to Japan". A person is "en japaner" and the language is "japansk". It is spelled the same as in English, but said with Danish sounds.

sentence.en: My friend is travelling to Japan.

japansk.explanation: "Japansk" is the adjective, and it is written with a small letter in Danish, unlike "Japanese" in English. Add -e for more than one: "japanske". On its own, with no noun, it is also the name of the language: "Jeg taler japansk". A Japanese person is "en japaner".

sentence.en: I love Japanese food.

jeg.explanation: "Jeg" means I. Unlike English "I", it is not capitalised in the middle of a sentence, only at the start. It is said a bit like "yai", and the "g" is silent. Its other form is "mig" (me), used after a word like "til" or after the action: "Han ser mig" (He sees me). The word for "my" is "min", "mit" or "mine".

sentence.en: I live in Copenhagen.

jeg er enig.explanation: "Jeg er enig" means "I agree". Notice that Danish says "I am agreed", not "I agree" with a verb. Add "helt" for "completely" or "ikke" to disagree. The opposite word is "uenig". Use "enig med" before the person: "jeg er enig med dig".

sentence.en: I agree with you.

jeg er ked af det.explanation: This phrase means "I am sad", and also "I am sorry" when you regret something. Note the small word "af det" at the end; "jeg er ked" alone is incomplete. For a quick apology like bumping into someone, "undskyld" is more common. "Jeg er ked af det" sounds more heartfelt.

sentence.da: **Jeg er ked af det**, men jeg kan ikke komme i dag.
sentence.en: I'm sorry, but I can't come today.

jeg forstår ikke.explanation: "Jeg forstår ikke" means "I don't understand" and is very useful when you are learning. "Forstår" is the present form of "at forstå" (to understand), and "ikke" (not) comes after it. Add "det" for "it", as in "Jeg forstår det ikke". Together with "kan du gentage det?" (can you repeat that?), it will help you in many talks.

sentence.en: Sorry, I don't understand.

jeg har det godt.explanation: This is the usual answer to "hvordan har du det?" (how are you?). Danish says "have it good" where English says "be doing well", so "det" is needed. Do not say "jeg er godt", which sounds wrong. Add "rigtig" for "really well", or say "det går godt" (it's going well) for much the same idea.

sentence.da: Tak, **jeg har det godt**. Og dig?
sentence.en: Thanks, I'm doing well. And you?

jeg har det skidt.explanation: Use this when you feel unwell or are having a hard time. "Skidt" means badly or poorly, and the phrase works for feeling ill as well as feeling down. It is a bit informal and very common. A milder option is "jeg har det ikke så godt" (I'm not doing so well).

sentence.da: I dag **har jeg det skidt**, fordi jeg er syg.
sentence.en: Today I'm not doing well, because I'm sick.

forms.da: Hvad hedder du? Jeg hedder Lars.

jeg hedder….explanation: "Jeg hedder.." means "My name is.." and you add your name after it. It literally means "I am called..". The verb is "at hedde" (to be called), and it is the normal way to introduce yourself. Danes then usually say "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you). You do not use "jeg er" for your name, even though English uses "I am".

sentence.en: My name is Anna, and you?

jeg kommer fra….explanation: "Jeg kommer fra.." means "I'm from.." and you add a country or town after it. It literally means "I come from..". It is the usual answer to "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?). Use "jeg bor i.." (I live in..) for where you live now, because that is a different thing from where you come from.

sentence.en: I'm from Canada.

forms.da: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.
Jeg vil gerne have to billetter.

jeg vil gerne have.explanation: "Jeg vil gerne have" means "I would like" and is the polite way to order or ask for something. Put the thing you want after "have". "Gerne" softens it, so it sounds friendly, not demanding. Without "gerne", "jeg vil have" is blunt, like "I want".

sentence.da: **Jeg vil gerne have** en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

jer.explanation: "Jer" means "you" when you speak to more than one person and something is done to them, such as "Jeg kan se jer". When they are the ones doing it, you say "I". For one person the word is "dig". It is also used after words like "til" and "med".

sentence.en: I have a gift for you (all).

jeres.explanation: "Jeres" means "your" or "yours" when you speak to more than one person, as in "jeres hus". It never changes. For one person you use "din", "dit" or "dine". It comes from "I" and "jer".

sentence.en: Is that your car (you all)?

jo.explanation: "Jo" has two uses. It is "yes" when you answer a question with "not" in it: "Kommer du ikke?" "Jo!" ("Aren't you coming?" "Yes, I am!"). Inside a sentence it adds a feeling of "you know" or "of course", like "det er jo rigtigt". Use "ja" for ordinary yes answers.

sentence.da: Kan du ikke lide kaffe? **Jo**, det kan jeg.
sentence.en: Don't you like coffee? Yes, I do.

jord.explanation: Jord is earth in two senses: the soil that plants grow in, and the ground you stand on. It is an en-word, so "the earth" is "jorden". When it is written with a capital letter, "Jorden" is the planet we live on. "På jorden" means "on the ground" or "on earth". Inside a house you do not say "jord" for the floor, you say "gulv".

sentence.en: The plants grow in the soil.

juice.explanation: "Juice" is juice, an en-word, so "the juice" is "juicen". The word is borrowed from English but is said in a Danish way. People usually say what type it is, such as "appelsinjuice" (orange juice) or "æblejuice" (apple juice).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **juice** til morgenmad.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of juice for breakfast.

jul.explanation: "Jul" means Christmas and is an en-word, though you rarely use "en" with it. You say "til jul" (at Christmas) and "i julen" (during the Christmas season). The greeting is "Glædelig jul!". Jul is also the old Nordic midwinter feast, which is why Danes use this word and not a word like "Christ".

sentence.en: We celebrate Christmas at my grandmother's.

juleaften.explanation: "Juleaften" is Christmas Eve, the evening of the 24th of December. It is the most important day of Danish Christmas: families eat a big dinner, dance around the tree and open presents. It is an en-word but is normally used with no "en". You say "juleaften" or "juleaftensdag".

sentence.da: Vi spiser and hos mormor til **juleaften**.
sentence.en: We eat duck at grandmother's for Christmas Eve.

juli.explanation: "Juli" is July, written with a small letter. You say "i juli" for in July. It sounds close to "juni", so listen for the difference in the middle: "juli" has an l. July is the main summer holiday month for most Danes, and many places close.

sentence.en: Many Danes are on vacation in July.

juni.explanation: "Juni" is June, written with a small letter. You say "i juni" for in June. In Denmark June has very long, light evenings, and the midsummer festival "sankthans" is celebrated on 23 June with bonfires. Take care not to mix it up with "juli" (July), which sounds similar.

sentence.en: It stays light for a long time in June.
